title: The pointer
hook: the reader follows the words with a silver hand, so the scroll isn't touched

segments.voice: Yesterday, the aron kodesh opened and the room stood. Your line was stand for the scroll. Did you greet someone properly when they came in? Today, the scroll is open on the table, and a small silver hand appears. Day five hundred ninety-eight.

Here is the job description. Read aloud, in front of a full room, from a page with no punctuation, no vowels, no verse numbers, and no notes on how to sing it. Just columns of black Hebrew letters, written by hand on parchment, in a text the room expects to hear without a single word wrong. And no putting a finger on the line to keep your place. That's the Torah reader's job, week after week. And there's a small tool on the table to help, shaped like a hand.
screen: `NO VOWELS, NO PUNCTUATION.` → `NOT A SINGLE WORD WRONG.` → `A TOOL SHAPED LIKE A HAND.`

segments.voice: It's called a yad: Hebrew for hand. A slim rod, often silver, sometimes wood, ending in a tiny hand with one finger pointing. The reader holds it just above the parchment and moves it word by word. Why not just use a finger? Two reasons. First, the scroll itself is fragile, and treated as holy. Every letter is written by a trained scribe, a sofer, with a quill and special ink, and a smudged or broken letter can make the whole scroll unfit until it's repaired. Hands carry oil and sweat. Second, there's a teaching in the Talmud, in Megillah 32a, that holding a Torah scroll with bare hands is a kind of disrespect. So people touch it with something else: the fringe of a tallit, the cover, or the yad. The yad itself is a custom, not a law spelled out in the Talmud, but today it's a familiar sight at the reading table. Because the scroll has no vowels or musical notes, the reader prepares well ahead. In many synagogues, two people stand on either side, following in a printed book with all the vowels and notes, ready to quietly correct a mistake. And the person called up to bless the reading touches the place with their tallit fringe and kisses it. Notice what the yad teaches without a word. The point isn't the hand. It's what the hand points to. A good teacher, a good parent, a good friend works the same way.
screen: `YAD: A HAND THAT POINTS.` · `A SMUDGED LETTER, AN UNFIT SCROLL.` · `NO VOWELS, NO NOTES: PREPARED BY HEART.` · `THE POINT IS WHAT IT POINTS TO.` · then, large: `A HAND THAT POINTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: follow a text with your finger. Pick up something written: a book, a letter, a page of scripture, even a recipe. Choose a few lines. Read them slowly, moving your finger, or a pen, just under each word as you go. Don't let your eyes run ahead of your hand. Notice how much slower it is, and how much more you see: small words, odd spellings, a phrase you'd usually skim. If it's a sacred text for you, let the pointing be a kind of respect. The bell holds the time.
Yad. Hand. The pointer the Torah reader uses to follow the words without touching the parchment.
Your line: a hand that points. Today, when you help someone, point them toward the answer instead of handing it over. Day five hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: During the Torah reading, the reader follows the text with a yad, a pointer ending in a small hand, while gabbaim follow in a printed chumash and correct errors; those called up touch the scroll with a tallit fringe or its cover and kiss it.

fork.setup: you're reading Torah in front of the congregation and need to keep your place on the parchment. what do you do?
options: run your finger along the line.
follow the words with a yad, just above the parchment.
fork.reveal: the yad keeps your place without touching the parchment, protecting the letters and honoring the scroll.

original.note: Hebrew: hand. the name of the Torah pointer.

trapdoor: what you thought: a decorative silver stick.
what it means: a hand that points without touching, protecting the letters and keeping the reader's place.
what a scholar hears: Megillah 32a on not holding a scroll bare; the laws of a pasul scroll for damaged letters; the yad as minhag, not Talmudic law.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Tefillin, Mezuzah and Torah Scroll 7 and 10

notes: Megillah 32a: one who holds a Torah scroll naked (bare-handed) is buried naked (without the merit); confirm paraphrase as 'a kind of disrespect'.
Yad as custom rather than Talmudic requirement; confirm.
Damaged letters render a scroll pasul until repaired (Mishneh Torah, Sefer Torah 10); confirm citation.
Ending generalization ('a good teacher... works the same way') is an observation, not a sourced claim.
